You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.02 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.15 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.01 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor-node $R_L$ from a piezo transducer.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $V_{out,min} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$
        *   $V_{out,max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$
        *   $V_{pp} \le 0.02\text{ V}$ (ripple)
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.15\text{ s}$ (startup)
        *   $dv \le 0.01\text{ V}$ (settled)
    *   Piezo characteristics: $C_p = 25\text{ nF}$, $I_p = 50\text{ \mu A}$ (nominal), $f = 100\text{ Hz}$. Open circuit voltage $\approx 3.2\text{ V}$.
    *   Previous result (SSHI_FullBridge):
        *   High voltage output (passed $V_{out,min}$ and $V_{out,max}$).
        *   Fails startup: $t_{up}$ is too slow.
        *   Fails settled: $dv$ is too high.
        *   Fails ripple: $V_{pp}$ is too high.
        *   Observation: The storage capacitor $C_{out} = 4.7\text{ \mu F}$ is likely too large for fast startup but potentially too small or the power pulses are too sparse for low ripple/stability. Wait, the feedback says $C_{out}$ might be too large for startup but $V_{pp}$ is still high. This implies the power is delivered in large, infrequent chunks.

    *   SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor) significantly boosts the voltage by flipping the voltage across $C_p$.
    *   The current topology used `L1` and `S1` to flip $V_{C_p}$ (connecting $pzp \rightarrow L1 \rightarrow S1 \rightarrow pzn$).
    *   The rectifier is a full bridge (`D1-D4`).
    *   The problem with the full bridge is that it has 2 diode drops (roughly $0.5\text{ V}$ total for DSCH).
    *   The "settled" and "startup" failures suggest the time constant $\tau \approx R_L C_{out}$ is too large or the power is not being integrated efficiently.
    *   S2 (heavy load $150\text{ k}\Omega$) has $V_{pp} = 212\text{ mV}$. $S4$ (light load $1\text{ M}\Omega$) has $V_{pp} = 300\text{ mV}$. This is strange—usually, ripple is higher with heavier loads.
    *   Actually, looking at the SSHI_FullBridge result: $V_{avg}$ is high (often $> 3\text{ V}$), meaning it's pushing against the Zener clamp $DZ33$ ($3.3\text{ V}$). When the output is clamped at $3.3\text{ V}$, the "ripple" might be the oscillation of the clamp or the charging process.

    *   To improve startup time $t_{up}$, we need to deliver charge faster at low $V_{out}$.
    *   To improve ripple $V_{pp}$ and settling $dv$, we need a more stable charging mechanism or a better filter.
    *   The current SSHI flip happens on *both* edges.
    *   The full bridge rectifier has a high drop. Maybe a synchronous rectifier or a different topology? But we only have 4 switches.

    *   *Idea 1: Synchronous Rectification (Active Bridge).*
        Replace the bridge diodes with switches. But we only have 4 switches total. SSHI already uses one switch for the flip.
    *   *Idea 2: Parallel SSHI (Half-Bridge or different configuration).*
        Standard SSHI often uses a switch to short the piezo (flip) and a rectifier.
    *   *Idea 3: Improving the storage.*
        If the ripple is high and it takes too long to settle, the energy per cycle is high but delivered infrequently.
    *   *Idea 4: Use a different SSHI variant.*
        Instead of a full bridge, maybe a half-bridge if we can shift the ground? No, we can't.
    *   *Idea 5: Re-evaluate the "flip" mechanism.*
        The current L-S combination is $pzp \rightarrow L \rightarrow S \rightarrow pzn$. This flips $C_p$ voltage.
        Then $D1-D4$ rectifies.
        $D1: pzp \rightarrow out$, $D2: pzn \rightarrow out$, $D3: 0 \rightarrow pzp$, $D4: 0 \rightarrow pzn$.

    *   The SSHI_FullBridge is very powerful (screening showed $249\%$ to $951\%$ power). The failure is in the *dynamics* (startup, ripple, settling).
    *   High ripple and slow settling often happen when the output is clamped by the Zener. The Zener $DZ33$ is a hard limit. If the SSHI circuit tries to push $V_{out}$ to $5\text{ V}$, the Zener will clamp it, but the process might be "bursty".
    *   Wait, if $V_{avg} \approx 3.3\text{ V}$ and the Zener is at $3.3\text{ V}$, we are essentially operating the Zener in the breakdown region.
    *   To reduce ripple, we might need a larger capacitor, but that slows startup. This is the classic trade-off.
    *   However, $C_1 = 4.7\text{ \mu F}$ is already the maximum allowed.
    *   Maybe the problem is that the SSHI flip is *too* effective, creating massive spikes that the Zener can't smooth, or the energy is delivered in very high-voltage, low-charge pulses.

    *   What if we use a different rectifier? A voltage doubler (Greinacher/Dickson) might be too much voltage.
    *   What if we use a Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction (SECE) circuit? The previous SECE attempt failed the screen. Let's refine it.
    *   SECE typically uses an inductor to move charge.
    *   Let's try a "Half-Bridge SSHI" or a "Parallel-SSHI" where we don't use a full bridge.
    *   Actually, let's look at the "startup" fail. $t_{up} > 0.15\text{ s}$. This means $V_{out}$ takes too long to reach $1.8\text{ V}$.
    *   With a full bridge, we lose $\approx 0.5\text{ V}$.
    *   What if we use a switch-based rectifier?
        S1: $pzp \rightarrow out$ (when $pzp > out$)
        S2: $pzn \rightarrow out$ (when $pzn > out$)
        But we need to flip $C_p$ too.
        S3: $pzp \rightarrow L \rightarrow pzn$ (flip)

    *   Let's try a simpler structure: a "Buck-Boost" like approach or a "Charge Pump".
    *   Wait, the problem might be the $C_{out}$ value. If $C_{out}$ is too large, $t_{up}$ is slow. If it's too small, $V_{pp}$ is high. The tuner is already trying to optimize this.
    *   If the tuner can't find a value for $C_{out}$ that satisfies both, the topology itself is the problem.

    *   The current SSHI flips the voltage. This increases the voltage across the diodes.
    *   If we use a *Synchronous* Rectifier, we eliminate the $0.5\text{ V}$ drop, speeding up startup.
    *   Proposed Topology:
        S1: $pzp \rightarrow out$ (ctrl=G1, edges=pos)
        S2: $pzn \rightarrow out$ (ctrl=G2, edges=neg)
        S3: $pzp \rightarrow L1 \rightarrow pzn$ (ctrl=G3, edges=both)
        Wait, only 2 SYNC controllers are allowed.
    *   Alternative: use the SYNC to control the flip and use diodes for rectification.
    *   Wait, the SSHI_FullBridge already did this. The problem was $V_{pp}$ and $t_{up}$.
    *   Let's try a "Standard SSHI" with a *single* diode and a switch? No, the piezo is AC.

    *   Maybe the problem is the $L$ value? $L=10\text{ mH}$ is quite large.
    *   Let's try a different "flip" topology.
    *   What if we use the SECE approach again, but correctly?
        SECE:
        $C_{fly}$ (flying cap)
        S1: $pzp \rightarrow C_{fly}$
        S2: $C_{fly} \rightarrow out$
        This extracts charge when $V_{pzp}$ is peak.

    *   Let's try a "Synchronous Rectifier" using only 2 switches:
        S1: $pzp \rightarrow out$ (edges=pos)
        S2: $pzn \rightarrow out$ (edges=neg)
        And no inductor? This is just a synchronous rectifier. It won't boost.
        But we have the Zener. If we don't boost, we might not hit $1.8\text{ V}$ on S4 (weak excitation).
        S4: $I_p = 30\text{ \mu A}$, $V_{oc} \approx 1.9\text{ V}$.
        With a full bridge (0.5 V drop), $V_{out}$ will be $\approx 1.4\text{ V}$, which is why the FBR failed S4.

    *   SSHI is the right way to boost. Why did it fail $V_{pp}$ and $t_{up}$?
        $V_{pp}$ is the ripple. In the SSHI_FullBridge, the power was delivered in bursts.
        Maybe we should use a smaller inductor to make the pulses more frequent or shorter?
        Actually, the "ripple" is measured from 0.7 to 0.8 s.
        If $V_{out}$ is clamped at $3.3\text{ V}$, any pulse that pushes it above $3.3\text{ V}$ is chopped by the Zener, and then it decays via $R_L$ until the next pulse.
        $V_{ripple} \approx \Delta V = \frac{I_{pulse} \cdot \Delta t}{C_{out}}$.
        If the pulses are too large, $\Delta V$ is large.
        To reduce $\Delta V$, we need to:
        1. Increase $C_{out}$ (but this slows $t_{up}$).
        2. Decrease the energy per pulse (by reducing $L$ or $t_{on}$).
        3. Increase the frequency of pulses.

    *   Wait, if we use a *smaller* $L$, the flip is faster, and the voltage boost is lower. This might actually *help* the ripple and the Zener clamping.

    *   The a-priori best way to handle the $V_{oc} \approx 1.9\text{ V}$ (S4) and $V_{out,min} = 1.8\text{ V}$ is a low-drop interface.
    *   A synchronous rectifier (using switches) has almost zero drop.
    *   Let's try a "Synchronous SSHI" but we are limited to 2 SYNCs and 4 switches.
    *   Controller G1: `edges=both`, `phase=0`.
        S1: $pzp \rightarrow L \rightarrow pzn$ (Flip)
        This uses 1 SYNC.
    *   Now we need to rectify.
        D1: $pzp \rightarrow out$
        D2: $pzn \rightarrow out$
        D3: $0 \rightarrow pzp$
        D4: $0 \rightarrow pzn$
        This is exactly the SSHI_FullBridge.

    *   What if we change the rectifier to a *half-wave* rectifier with a charge pump?
        S1: $pzp \rightarrow L \rightarrow pzn$ (Flip)
        D1: $pzp \rightarrow C_{mid}$
        D2: $C_{mid} \rightarrow out$
        D3: $pzp \rightarrow out$
        This is a voltage doubler. It might be too much.

    *   Let's try to improve the SSHI_FullBridge by removing the Zener? No, we need to prevent $V_{out} > 3.6\text{ V}$.
    *   What if we use a smaller $C_{out}$ to help $t_{up}$, and see if the tuner can fix the ripple?
        The tuner already tried $C_{out}$ from $1\text{e-10}$ to $4.7\text{e-05}$.
        If $C_{out} = 4.7\text{ \mu F}$ was used, it's because the tuner was trying to fix the ripple.

    *   What if we use a "Synchronous Rectifier" for the positive half and a "Diode Rectifier" for the negative? No.
    *   How about this:
        S1: $pzp \rightarrow out$ (ctrl=G1, edges=pos)
        S2: $pzn \rightarrow out$ (ctrl=G2, edges=neg)
        This is a synchronous rectifier.
        To handle the voltage boost, we can add an inductor in series with the switches?
        S1: $pzp \rightarrow L1 \rightarrow out$ (ctrl=G1, edges=pos)
        S2: $pzn \rightarrow L2 \rightarrow out$ (ctrl=G2, edges=neg)
        This looks like a boost converter.

    *   Actually, let's try a "Parallel SSHI" (also known as P-SSHI).
        In P-SSHI, the flip happens *before* the rectification.
        Wait, the SSHI_FullBridge already does that.

    *   Let's look at the "settled" failure. $dv$ is the difference between the mean of $0.6-0.7\text{ s}$ and $0.7-0.8\text{ s}$.
        If it's not settled, the capacitor is still charging (or discharging).
        This happens if the power delivered is very close to the power consumed, or if the time constant is very large.
        $R_L C_{out}$ for $S2 (150\text{ k}\Omega)$ and $C_{out} (4.7\text{ \mu F})$ is $\approx 0.7\text{ s}$.
        This is why it's not settled by $0.8\text{ s}$!
        The time constant is too long.
        To fix this, we need a smaller $C_{out}$.
        But a smaller $C_{out}$ increases ripple $V_{pp}$.
        This is the core conflict.

    *   To have small ripple AND a small time constant, we need the power to be delivered more *continuously* rather than in large pulses.
    *   The current SSHI delivers energy in huge bursts every half-cycle.
